teaser.en: Long before toothpaste, coastal people cleaned their teeth with a chewed twig from this tree, and many still do.

summary.en: *Msuwaki* is the toothbrush tree, a drooping, pale-leaved shrub of dry bush and riverbanks. Its twigs and roots are the original toothbrush of the coast, and the word *mswaki* now means any toothbrush.

about.en: *Msuwaki* is an evergreen shrub or small tree with drooping, sometimes trailing branches. Its leaves are pale green and slightly fleshy. Small pink-purple berries follow the tiny flowers. The twigs and roots have a sharp, peppery taste.

where.en: It grows in coastal and dry lowland bushland and along river banks.

uses.en: Twigs and roots are used as toothbrushes: the end is chewed until it frays into bristles, and then rubbed over the teeth. The peppery fruit is eaten, the roots and bark are used in traditional medicine, and the leaves are fodder for livestock.

culture.en: The tree gave its name to the toothbrush itself: in Swahili, *mswaki* means a toothbrush of any kind, and the chewing stick is still a common sight on the coast.

names.en: In Digo it is *msuwaki* or *mswaki*. The Swahili, Giriama and Chonyi name is *mswaki*. In English it is the toothbrush tree; it is also known worldwide as miswak. Pakia notes that another tree, *Dobera loranthifolia*, is also called *msuwaki*.

reason.en: Horsewood, whose twigs are also used as toothbrushes
African myrrh, also used for toothbrushes
Grows in the same dry bushland

sources: Pakia, M. (2005) African Traditional Plant Knowledge Today: an ethnobotanical study of the Digo at the Kenya Coast. PhD thesis, Univ. Bayreuth, Appendix III (Digo–botanical name list) & Appendix VI (name semantics). https://epub.uni-bayreuth.de/881/1/Pakia.pdf
